beginner.headline: Rare Beetle Found Again in Wales
beginner.brief: A rare beetle, a type of insect, was found in Pembrokeshire, Wales, after 60 years. It is called the Short-Necked Oil Beetle. Last year, people found only dead adult beetles at a place called Castlemartin. This year, experts found very young beetles there after three years of searching. Anne Hobbs said the beetles may be having young in Wales again. These beetles need certain bees to survive. They also need many flowers and plants to hide in. They can live in grassy places near the sea. They move around most on warm, sunny days. Castlemartin is the only place in Wales where people can find these beetles now.

intermediate.headline: Rare Beetle Found Again in Wales After 60 Years
intermediate.brief: A rare beetle has been discovered in Pembrokeshire after being missing from Wales for 60 years. In the past, habitat loss had brought the Short-Necked Oil Beetle close to extinction, meaning it could have disappeared completely. Last year, a survey at Castlemartin found only dead adult beetles, raising concerns about the species' future there. This year, after three years of searching, experts discovered larvae, or young beetles at an early stage of development, in a small area. Anne Hobbs from the Bumblebee Conservation Trust said the evidence suggested that the species was breeding in Wales again. The beetles are dependent on bees to complete their life cycle and need a particular habitat, or type of natural environment. They need thick plants for shelter and plenty of flowers in their habitat. They are usually seen from March to June in coastal grassland and sand dunes, especially on warm, sunny days. Because they need such specific conditions, only a handful of sites in the UK are suitable for them. Castlemartin Range is currently the only known site for the species in Wales, and wildlife protection workers regularly survey it. Hobbs said protection work needed to consider the needs of several species to be effective. She thanked the project's partners and volunteers for continuing their support, despite two years without any sightings of larvae.

advanced.headline: Rediscovered Beetle Shows Signs of Reproducing in Wales
advanced.brief: The short-necked oil beetle has been rediscovered in Pembrokeshire after an apparent absence of 60 years from Wales. Recent surveys had prompted fears of local extinction, meaning that the beetle might no longer exist in Wales. Across the UK, the species went unreported for almost 60 years after 1948, as habitat loss brought it to the brink of extinction. Last year's survey at Castlemartin recorded only dead adults, prompting concern about the species' persistence at the site. After three years of searching, experts discovered larvae, or immature beetles, in a small area of the site, suggesting that they had located part of a larger batch of young beetles. According to Natural Resources Wales, the number and distribution of the larvae corroborated this interpretation. Anne Hobbs, from the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, welcomed indications that the species was reproducing in Wales again. The beetle relies on solitary bees for its life cycle and requires both thick vegetation for cover and abundant flowers. Natural Resources Wales said these exacting habitat requirements leave only a few suitable sites in the UK. The species is classified as nationally rare in Great Britain and is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. The beetles are typically encountered between March and June in coastal grassland rich in flowers and in sand dunes, with activity greatest on warm, sunny days. Rediscoveries elsewhere in the UK included Devon in 2006 and the Isle of Coll in Scotland in 2009. Castlemartin Range remains the species' only known Welsh location and is subject to sustained monitoring by conservationists. The work forms part of Wales's flagship species recovery programme, which also seeks to conserve other species sharing similar habitats. Hobbs stressed that effective conservation must accommodate the needs of several species.
